n: This topic is devoted to thanatology and terminal states. The term thanatology was introduced into medicine by I. I. Mechnikov: thanatos, the god of death, and logos, doctrine. Forensic medical thanatology studies questions of death in order to resolve the tasks of the inquiry, investigation and court. The sequence of terminal states is as follows: pre-agony, terminal pause, agony, clinical death and biological death.

Now the first three stages of the terminal states. In pre-agony, the higher parts of the central nervous system are inhibited, circulation and respiration are disturbed, and acidosis and hypoxia develop. It lasts from several minutes to several days. In the terminal pause, breathing suddenly stops, and the pupils dilate and do not react to light; this lasts from several seconds to 3-4 minutes. In agony, breathing is restored and arterial pressure rises. At the end, first breathing and then the heart stops, and the face changes, the facies hippocratica.

Clinical death begins after the heartbeat stops. Under ordinary conditions it lasts up to 5-6 minutes, and at low temperature up to 30 minutes. After 5-6 minutes, irreversible changes develop in the cerebral cortex. In biological death, irreversible changes occur in organs and tissues, above all in the brain. That is, clinical death is still a reversible period, while biological death is an irreversible state.

t: Four types of agony (Lawes and Berg)
n: By duration, agony is divided into four types. Rapid death is observed mainly in electrical injury, mechanical asphyxia and anaphylactic shock, while slow death is related to various diseases. W. Lawes and S. Berg in 1965 distinguished four types of agony. The agonyless type occurs in an instant and is incompatible with life. Short agony lasts 4-5 minutes and occurs in asphyxia and electrical injury. Prolonged agony lasts hours and days and occurs in disease and trauma. Artificially prolonged agony is extended by medical measures to weeks, months, years.

The term euthanasia was introduced in the 16th century by F. Bacon. It means a good death, and its underlying essence is the relief of the suffering of patients doomed to die. Active euthanasia is hastening death by an action. Passive euthanasia, that is, orthothanasia, is limiting or stopping help. Medicothanasia is relieving suffering with drugs, and dysthanasia is prolonging life to the maximum by radical measures.

t: Establishing that death has occurred: brain death
n: In establishing that death has occurred, the concept of brain death is important. Irreversible changes occur first in the cerebral cortex. Its death is accepted as the beginning of biological death, that is, "brain death". The interval between the death of the cerebral cortex and the death of other organs is close to 20 hours; transplantation is based on this. Brain death is established in the prescribed manner, usually by a qualified resuscitation specialist and neurologists. If that is not possible, it is established from cadaveric changes.

t: Early and reliable signs of death
n: Signs of death are divided into early and reliable groups. Early signs: immobility, pallor, absence of consciousness, respiration and heartbeat, some cooling. Although they are detected immediately after death, they are of a probable nature. The earliest reliable sign is the Beloglazov symptom, that is, the "cat's eye"; it appears after 15-20 minutes; in 1.5-2.0 hours the pupillary muscles stiffen, and it may not be detected. Reliable signs also include cooling of the body to 23 degrees and below, and also cadaveric lividity, rigor and drying.

Forensic medical classification of death. From the forensic medical point of view, the category, kind and type of death are distinguished. By category, death may be violent, that is, from external action, or non-violent, that is, from diseases. The kinds of violent death: homicide, suicide and accident. The types of violent death are related to mechanical injury, asphyxia, poisoning, and the action of temperature and electricity.

Supravital reactions. In the first period after brain death, some organs and tissues respond to external action. These reactions are used in determining the time of death. With mechanical action, in 1-2 hours the limb muscles contract, and up to 10 hours an "idiomuscular swelling", that is, a ridge, appears at the site of action. With electric current, in 2-3 hours the muscles of the face, neck and limbs contract, and in 3-5 hours the orbicularis oris. Up to 11-12 hours only the eye muscles contract.

Cadaveric changes are divided into two groups. Early changes occur in the first day: cooling, drying, cadaveric lividity, rigor and autolysis. Late changes begin from the second day. They are divided into destructive and preservative types. Destructive ones include putrefaction and the action of insects, animals, birds and fish. Preservative ones include mummification, adipocere, peat tanning and freezing.

Cooling of the body. Thermoregulation is disturbed, heat production stops, while heat loss continues. Therefore the body cools until it equalises with the temperature of the environment. The degree of cooling is determined by touch and thermometry: mouth, armpit, chest cavity, rectum, liver. Under room conditions the body temperature falls by about one degree in an hour. The temperature equalises after 16 hours in the armpit, 19 in the rectum, and 25 in the liver.

t: Drying of the body and parchment patches
n: Drying of the body is related to the cessation of glandular function and evaporation of moisture. It is observed first in moist places: the red border of the lips, mucous membranes and the cornea. In 1-3 hours the cornea clouds, and in 4-5 hours a triangular brownish-brown Larcher spot appears on the conjunctiva. Parchment patches are yellowish-brown and firm. If warm moistened gauze is applied to them for 5-10 minutes, they soften and become pale. A vital abrasion, however, does not change, which is how they are distinguished.

The mechanism of rigor mortis has not been fully elucidated. At present most link it with the breakdown of adenosine triphosphate, that is, ATP. When ATP is exhausted, the muscles stiffen; contractures from increased calcium in the muscles are also important. ATP disappears completely 10-12 hours after death. Rigor is detected after 1-3 hours: first in the masticatory muscles, then in the muscles of the neck, trunk and limbs, that is, a descending type, Nysten's law. After 12-16 hours it is in all muscles, after 24 hours it is maximal, and in 3-7 days it disappears completely.

Features and factors of rigor. Cataleptic rigor develops immediately after death in all muscles. It is observed in death from injury of the medulla oblongata or cervical spinal cord, from convulsant poisons or from a convulsive disease. Rigor of the heart muscle develops after 2 hours, this is "post-mortem systole", and disappears after 5-6 hours. At low temperature, in children and the elderly, and in cachexia, rigor is weak. At high temperature, in strong musculature and in strychnine poisoning it develops quickly and strongly.

Cadaveric lividity passes through three stages. Cadaveric lividity is the visibility through the skin of blood accumulated in the skin and subcutaneous fat; in internal organs it is called hypostasis. Hypostasis appears in 1.5-2 hours and lasts up to 8-12 hours. On pressure it disappears and is quickly restored. If the position is changed, it appears in the new place. Stasis occurs in 12-24 hours; on pressure it blanches and is slowly restored. Imbibition develops later, and on pressure the colour does not change.

t: Site and colour of cadaveric lividity
n: Site and colour of cadaveric lividity. The location depends on the position of the body after death: if it lies on its back, on the posterior and lateral surfaces; if face down, on the anterior and lateral parts. In rapid death the patches are diffuse, dark reddish-bluish and appear quickly. In agonal death they are late and indistinct. With heavy blood loss, islets are seen after 3-4 hours. The colour also depends on the poison: with carbon monoxide pinkish-red, with cyanides cherry, with substances forming methaemoglobin brownish-brown.

t: Distinguishing cadaveric lividity from a bruise
n: It is important to distinguish cadaveric lividity from a bruise. Cadaveric lividity lies in low-lying areas; its shape is indefinite, without borders, and it merges. In hypostasis and stasis it disappears or blanches on pressure. Bruises have a definite shape and borders, do not merge, and do not change colour on pressure; those inflicted earlier are greenish-yellow. In a doubtful area, a cruciform incision is made. In a patch, drops of blood or exuded fat are found, while in a bruise there is clotted blood extravasated into the tissue.

Autolysis. After death, the activity of lysosomal and other proteolytic enzymes does not disappear at once, and the tissues digest themselves. In tissues rich in enzymes it proceeds faster: the gastrointestinal mucosa, the pancreas, the adrenal medulla, the thymus and the kidneys. Remember: autolysis of the gastric mucosa can be mistaken for the action of a corrosive poison. Autolytic and vital changes are distinguished microscopically.

Putrefaction is the breakdown of organic compounds, including proteins, under the action of microorganisms; it occurs mainly under the action of aerobic bacteria. At +20...+40 °C it proceeds well, at sub-zero temperature and above +55 °C it stops, and at 0...+10 °C it is very slow. A body putrefies two times more slowly in water and eight times more slowly in earth than in air, the Casper ratio 1:2:8. Heavy blood loss, dehydration, some poisonings, that is, carbon monoxide and arsenic, and taking antibiotics slow putrefaction. In death from sepsis and purulent processes the body putrefies faster; stout people putrefy faster than thin ones.

Signs of putrefaction appear in succession. On day 1 an odour is noticed. Green discoloration appears from the formation of sulphaemoglobin: on the second day in the right iliac region, in the second week over the whole skin. The putrefactive venous network is visible on days 3-4. Gases form cadaveric emphysema, in which crepitation is felt. From days 4-6, putrefactive blisters appear.

Types and timing of putrefaction. The gaseous type occurs in death from infectious diseases and sepsis. The moist type occurs in diseases in which fluid accumulates, and the dry type in cachexia, for example in cancer and tuberculosis. At room temperature putrefaction reaches its height in the second week; in the third month the soft tissues turn into a semi-liquid mass, and in the sixth month the body becomes skeletonised. Tissues more resistant to putrefaction: hair, bone, teeth, cartilage, ligaments and large blood vessels. Those that putrefy faster: stomach, intestine, liver, spleen, blood and brain.

Destruction by insects. Houseflies lay eggs around natural openings and wounds soon after death. At room temperature larvae appear after 24-30 hours. In favourable conditions the soft tissues of an adult body are destroyed by larvae down to the skeleton in 4-6 weeks, in children in 1-2 weeks. The sequence of insect development is used in determining the time of death: the necrophagous beetle appears in 30-45 days, the predatory beetle in 45-60 days.

Preservative changes are of three kinds. Mummification is late drying of the body; it develops in hot, dry, well-ventilated conditions, and putrefaction stops. In adults complete mummification takes 6-12 months, in children 4-6 months, in exceptionally favourable conditions 2-3 months. Traces of injuries and the possibility of establishing identity are preserved. Adipocere, that is, saponification, forms in watery or moist, airless or low-air, relatively cold conditions: hydrolysis of fat, glycerol is released, and fatty acids turn into soap. It begins after 2-3 months; in adults it is complete in 10-12 months, in children in 4-5 months. In peat tanning, under the action of humic acids the skin becomes dense and dark brown, the bones soften, and the body is preserved for many years.

Artificial changes of the body are also divided into two groups. Preservative changes include embalming: an equal mixture of ethyl alcohol and formalin is injected into the femoral artery. Storage in cold conditions is also in this group. Destructive changes include dismemberment: defensive dismemberment is to conceal a crime, offensive dismemberment is for revenge or insult. There are also burning and dissolving. To burn the body of an adult completely, 20 hours are needed, and for young children 2-3 hours.

t: Determining the time of death: rectal thermometry
n: Determination of the time of death is resolved on the basis of cadaveric changes, supravital reactions and laboratory tests; in practice cooling and cadaveric lividity are used more often. The rectal temperature is measured at the scene and at the examination. By measuring at least twice, at a definite interval, the time is determined from the degree of cooling. Example: at 10 o'clock it was +30 °C, at 12 o'clock +28.2 °C. In two hours it cooled by 1.8 °C, 0.9 hour corresponds to one degree, so death occurred 7-7.5 hours ago.

t: Time of death from lividity and laboratory
n: Time of death from cadaveric lividity and the laboratory. The cadaveric patches are pressed with a force of 196 kPa, that is, 2 kg/cm², for 3 seconds, and the time of colour recovery is measured, the Kononenko table. The potassium content increases in the cerebrospinal fluid and the vitreous body of the eye, and sodium decreases. Glycogen in the liver disappears by the end of the first day. Signs of autolysis in internal organs appear after 12-18 hours and become very marked in 36-48 hours. There is no single reliable method, so as many methods as possible are used.

t: Forensic medical examination of a body: when it is ordered
n: When is a forensic medical examination of a body ordered? On the basis of a resolution or ruling of the inquiry, investigation and court, it is carried out when there are signs of violence or suspicion of it. Cases of ordering: all kinds of violent death; suspicion of violent death; death of unknown persons; complaint about medical care previously provided. The examination begins only after early cadaveric signs have appeared. Putrefaction, however, does not prevent the examination.

Stages of the examination. First the materials submitted are studied: the resolution, the record of inspection and medical documents. After that an examination plan is drawn up. Then the external and internal examination of the body is carried out: the three main cavities, that is, cranial, thoracic and abdominal, are opened in any case. Then the diagnosis and certificate, laboratory examination, and finally the conclusions.

The expert's conclusion consists of three parts: introduction, investigation and a final part, that is, the findings. The introduction and the investigation together are called the descriptive part. The forensic medical diagnosis is drawn up on the pathogenetic principle: the main injury or disease, its complication and concomitant diseases. The diagnosis and findings are signed only by the expert. The conclusion is drawn up in at least two copies: one for the person who ordered it, and the other kept in the archive.

Thanatogenesis and causes of death. The mechanism by which death arises is called thanatogenesis; it is a chain of causes and effects. The first link of the chain is called the remote cause, those in the middle the intermediate cause, and the last the immediate cause. That is, the process leading to death begins with the remote cause and reaches the immediate cause through intermediate links.

Competition of causes of death. If there are two or more nosological forms, each of which could on its own lead to death, competition of remote causes arises. Example: if a victim who received a severe head injury in a road traffic accident is thrown into water, the head injury and drowning compete. The examination tries to determine the main nosological form. Only in exceptional cases are two remote causes stated.

We will consider an unknown, dismembered and skeletonised body. For the body of an unknown person a "verbal portrait" is drawn up: race, shape of head, hair, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, teeth and facial wrinkles. For a dismembered body, questions are posed: whether the parts are human, whether they belong to one person, sex, age, cause and time of death, weapon and age of injury. From a skeleton, sex, age and stature are determined. The cause of death usually cannot be established, but diatom plankton and some poisons may be found in the bones.

Exhumation. Removing a body from a grave is called exhumation. It is a procedural action carried out on the basis of a separate resolution or ruling. Lay witnesses and a forensic medicine specialist take part in the process, and the inquiry officer or investigator draws up a record. Besides lawful exhumation there is accidental, that is, during excavation work, and criminal, that is, theft and desecration.

t: Forensic medical and pathological anatomical examination
n: We distinguish forensic medical and pathological anatomical examination. A forensic medical examination is carried out to confirm or exclude signs of violence, and a pathological anatomical examination to check the correctness of treatment. A forensic medical examination is ordered by a resolution of the inquiry officer or investigator or a ruling of the court, and a pathological anatomical one by the order of the head of the medical institution. A forensic medical examination is a procedural action, the expert is warned of liability, and the result is the expert's conclusion. In a pathological anatomical examination the result is drawn up as a record.

Types of autopsy and burial. True, verbal and virtual autopsy are distinguished. In verbal autopsy the body is not opened; in virtual autopsy tomography is used, so far only in scientific institutions. Releasing a body from medical, pathological anatomical and forensic medical institutions without a medical certificate of death is prohibited. If a forensic medical or pathological anatomical examination is necessary, the body is released for burial no later than one day. If there are difficulties, it is kept in the mortuary for up to three days.

The concept of the scene. The scene is the place where the event occurred and the area where the body, weapon and other physical evidence were found. The place where the event occurred and the place where the body was found may sometimes be different. Inspection is an important and urgent procedural action, laid down in Articles 137 and 138 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Inspection of the body is a component of it.

Participants and types of inspection. Inspection is carried out with the participation of lay witnesses and a forensic medicine specialist. If there is no specialist, another doctor takes part; this is Article 70 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. A supplementary inspection is carried out when there are new circumstances or an object that was not fully studied, and a repeat inspection when the initial examination was of poor quality. In the centrifugal method the body is inspected first, then the surroundings; little effort is spent, but traces may be trampled. In the centripetal method the surroundings are inspected first, then the body; traces are preserved, but more time is needed.

t: Static and dynamic stage; the specialist's tasks
n: Inspection consists of two stages. In the static stage the objects are studied without changing their position. In the dynamic stage they can be moved and turned, and the body is studied more fully. The specialist records the fact of death, assists orderly inspection, cooperates in finding biological evidence and recording it in the record. He also advises on subsequent examinations, that is, on objects and questions.

t: Status and equipment of the specialist
n: Status and equipment of the specialist. The specialist does not have the status of a forensic expert. He does not give a written document, including an expert's conclusion; his opinions are oral and preliminary, tentative. He may express an opinion on the time of death, whether the position of the body has been changed, the character of the injury, the injuring object and the age of the injury. His case contains a gown, gloves, a magnifying glass, a thermometer, a stopwatch, a neurological hammer, atropine, pilocarpine, a measuring tape, test tubes and first aid supplies.

t: Procedure for inspecting the body at the scene
n: Procedure for inspecting the body at the scene. The first task is to record the fact of death. If there are signs of life or doubt, medical aid is given and the patient is sent to a medical institution. Clothing and footwear are not completely removed at the scene; they are described in detail, then areas of the body are inspected locally. Early changes are studied with the time and ambient temperature indicated. Rectal thermometry is carried out at least 2 times at an interval of one hour.

The record of inspection is drawn up by the inquiry officer or investigator; this is Article 141 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It consists of an introduction, a descriptive part and a final part. In the descriptive part, what was found is recorded in the order of inspection and in the state in which it was observed. The record is signed by the participants, including the specialist. It is drawn up in at least two copies, one being sent to the institution with the resolution for the examination.

t: Inspection in particular kinds of death
n: In particular kinds of death, inspection has its own features. In hanging, the body is not taken from the noose; the position, type, knot, height of attachment and auxiliary means are recorded; a non-slip noose is cut without disturbing the knot. In drowning, control samples of one litre each are taken for diatom plankton from three layers of the water body, that is, the surface, middle and bottom. In poisoning, a foreign odour, vomit, medicines, syringes and vessels are taken into account. In gas poisoning, the sanitary-epidemiological service takes air samples.
